text: You press Finish, and nothing happens until you tell an agent session:
I submitted.
Then you watch it build.
The GitHub Action in this repo starts on a push of plan dot resolved
dot M D, but the agent writes that file when it records your review.
By then, the work is done.
The second cost is the voice.
Rebuilding 2 frames of the system video re-narrated all 35 lines,
and took 11 minutes.
33 of them came out byte for byte the same.
And the system video is watch-only.
You can comment on it, but the review has nowhere to go:
intake takes only a plan's review,
and the system video has no plan.
So the plan makes 3 changes.
Rebuilds get cheap: step 1.
The loop runs itself: steps 2 and 3.
The system video can be reviewed:
step 4.
None of them needs the others.
Step 5 then proves all 3,
on real reviews.
Step 1: narrate only the lines that changed.
Each line's audio and word timings are kept under a key:
its text, the voice, the speed and the model.
On a rebuild, only new or edited lines go to the voice;
the rest are reused.
That update would have narrated 2 lines,
not 35: about 40 seconds, not 11 minutes.
Before anything runs, reel status says what an update costs in lines.
Next, part 2: the loop runs itself.
Part 2 of 3: steps 2 and 3,
and a question your review has since decided.
Who runs the loop was decided in your review:
a background agent.
Steps 2 and 3 are how.
Step 2: one main session, the one you talk to,
runs the work, but never sits on a long job.
It hands each one to a background worker:
build a video, implement a part,
check the code, fix a flag.
It checks what comes back and commits,
and reelplanning itself notifies you, under any agent.
Step 3 needs step 2.
When you press Finish, the review reaches the main session:
from the hosted page, Claude only,
through its hook; from the local page,
through the review server the session waits on.
Only if no session is open does the server start a fresh,
headless run: claude dash p, codex exec,
or opencode run.
Nothing is lost: the repo's reelplanning folder is the memory.
How far the first version goes beyond Claude Code was decided in your review:
one setting, tested with Claude Code.
The config names claude dash p;
changing that one line runs Codex or opencode instead.
Next, part 3: what a review of the system video can change.
Part 3 of 3: step 4,
the system video, and step 5,
the proof.
Step 4: reviewing the system video changes the system.
Each frame names its spec section and its parts,
so a comment lands on those parts.
If the video is wrong, the agent fixes the spec or the frame,
and rebuilds only that frame.
If the system itself should change,
it goes the way your review decided.
A small change inside one part goes straight in,
and you see it in a short walkthrough.
Anything with a choice becomes a plan first.
Step 5 needs all 4.
The GitHub Action and its template are removed,
and the docs say how the loop runs.
Then 2 real reviews, of this plan's walkthrough and of the system video,
are timed from Finish to the notification.
That is round one: 3 changes in 5 steps,
all built, and every question decided.
Next, round 2, from your review of its walkthrough.
Round 2.
The first 5 steps are built,
and your review of their walkthrough added 5 more,
with 4 open questions.
They make 3 changes.
A run nobody is watching gets the right powers:
step 6.
Reviews ask where you might disagree,
and stop only where it matters:
steps 7 and 8.
And less scaffolding: step 9.
None of them needs the others.
Step 10 then proves them on the next plan.
Step 6: what a run nobody is watching may do.
Nobody is there to answer a permission prompt,
so anything that would prompt is refused.
Today the run may edit files and run any shell command,
but not start workers, read the web or use MCP tools,
and nothing fences what a command touches.
This step picks the setting, and re-runs the step 5 proof with it.
What may that run do?
A: as now, edits and any shell command.
B: auto mode in the sandbox:
a classifier approves each action, workers and the web included.
C: everything, with the sandbox as the only fence.
D: a short list of commands,
still no workers.
I recommend B: the run can do what the main session does,
a classifier sits where you would,
and the sandbox bounds a mistake.
Which one?
Step 7: more quick checks.
A quick check asks you to predict what the plan or the code will
do, so a wrong answer marks a place where you expected something else.
Today a 6-minute walkthrough asks 2.
After any answer, a box asks how it should work,
and your words reach the agent as a comment on that step.
The box is built; this step decides how many checks,
and of what kind.
How many quick checks does a video ask?
A: at least one per step,
about one a minute.
B: one wherever there is something to predict;
could be 2, could be 12.
C: A's floor, plus B's.
I recommend C: the floor means no step goes unchecked,
which B alone cannot promise, and the extra checks go where a wrong answer
is most likely, which A alone never adds.
Which one?
Next, part 5: which of the agent's calls stop the video,
and how much scaffolding comes out.
Part 5: step 8, fewer stops;
step 9, less scaffolding; and step 10,
the proof.
Step 8: stop only for the calls you might overturn.
Across 4 walkthroughs, you accepted 68 of the agent's 71 calls as they were,
while 3 of 12 plan questions got your own words.
So the agent tags a call when it logs it:
visible, hard to undo, a deviation,
or close.
A tagged call stops the video,
as today.
Quick check.
The agent logs a call with no tag:
a heartbeat every 2 seconds.
What happens to it?
Untagged calls share one beat at the end of their part:
accept them all, or flag any one.
So does your own record also decide what stops?
A: the tags only.
B: the tags and your record:
a tag you accepted 10 times running no longer stops on its own,
and one flag brings it back.
C: every call still stops.
I recommend B: it starts as A,
and your verdicts, not a guess,
decide what fades.
Which one?
Step 9: less scaffolding.
A fresh agent audited the skill:
an agent reads about 12,000 words before it starts.
The tools that do mechanical work stay:
narration, captions, verify, plan diff, the review server,
the ledger guard.
What goes is text that only dictates format,
and what is said twice: a review,
for one, is kept 3 times.
How much comes out?
A: only what hurts, such as the exact step heading reel check demands;
small and safe, but the text stays as long.
B: A, and the skill and the style guide rewritten,
about half as long.
C: B, and the files: one build command,
and a review kept once.
I recommend C: format rules and duplicate files are what an agent spends its
attention on.
Which one?
Step 10 needs 6 to 9.
The next plan through the loop,
the Bob Dylan site redone from scratch,
uses the new quick checks and the call filter.
Its review counts the quick checks answered wrong,
and what each changed, and the stops against the calls you accepted without stopping.
That is round 2: 5 more steps,
and 4 questions.
Answer them, draw on any step to leave a note,
or approve.
